title: Where it grows
subtitle: Santorini and beyond
objectives: Name other Greek regions for Assyrtiko

steps.title: Santorini
steps.body: Assyrtiko's home is Santorini, a volcanic island in the Aegean, formed by a huge eruption around 1600 BC. Its soil, called aspa, is volcanic ash, pumice and lava, with almost no clay or organic matter. Rainfall is very low, about 300 mm a year; vines rely on night sea mist for moisture. Strong winds blow constantly.

steps.title: Phylloxera-free
steps.body: Santorini's volcanic sand doesn't let phylloxera survive, so the vines are ungrafted. Some root systems are over 400 years old: growers cut old vines back and let new shoots grow from the same roots. Assyrtiko also grows in mainland Greece, Macedonia and Crete, and in Australia's Clare Valley.

steps.title: Partners
steps.body: On Santorini, Assyrtiko is often blended with Athiri and Aidani, two aromatic local grapes. Santorini PDO must be at least 75% Assyrtiko. Single-vineyard and old-vine bottlings, like Nykteri, made from grapes picked at night, are increasingly common.

options: Phylloxera can't survive in its volcanic soil
steps.explanation: Phylloxera can't survive in Santorini's volcanic sand.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Santorini's volcanic aspa soil and sea mist shape Assyrtiko
Ungrafted roots can be over 400 years old
It also grows in mainland Greece, Crete and Australia
